source_title: Freakish frocks and ghoulish guises: last-minute Halloween costumes that won’t haunt the environment

The thrill of an event like Halloween doesn’t come from a brand new costume or “two pillowcases’ worth of sweets”, says play specialist Cat Sewell.
The fun comes from carving out the time to play, making ridiculous outfits, and the terror and delight of haunting the neighbourhood, says the artistic director and co-CEO of Polyglot Theatre, a company that creates participatory, immersive, child-led theatre.
“The value is the community connection, and the risk and scared-ness of knocking on doors, and doing that in a community. And the takeover of the streets again for families.”
Keen to join in the Halloween revelry but don’t have a costume? Experts say it’s not too late; you can still fashion a ghoulish get-up, without buying – or wasting – anything.
A great costume relies on a “sense of fun and commitment”, says Kristen Ahern, the founder of Conscious Costume. There are plenty of ways to use what you’ve already got, and avoid the trap of plastic dress-ups that tend to be bought new, worn once and thrown away.
“The commodification of Halloween is where the real problems lie,” Ahern says. “Thinking outside of franchises and characters that someone else has created really can open up a sense of freedom.”
Instead of being limited by pop culture, consider inventing your own fantastical creation from the dress-up box of simple materials, she says. You don’t have to buy “the perfect paper” or “perfect fabric” from a craft store, just use what you already have at home.
“Think about the essence of the character, or thing you want to be, and find ways to create that [with] what you have.”
You could be a nature spirit, by wearing green and gluing or taping on some leaves, she says. Or, embody an animal by dressing all in one colour and adding a tail and some ears. “You can do a lot with a wire coat hanger and some construction paper, or a brown grocery bag. Put those things together and you can make yourself some animal ears.”
The style trend known as “DisneyBounding” may be another source of inspiration. The idea developed as a way for adult Disney fans to dress up when visiting the theme park, and involves wearing garments that emulate the colour and style of a favourite character, but without the full costume. Ahern offers an example: “If they want to be Peter Pan, they’re wearing all green, and maybe a baseball cap that says Lost Boys on it.”
A clever costume doesn’t need to be complicated or expensive. Ahern recently attended a “wedding-ween”, where everyone dressed in costume. “Someone had a T-shirt on that said ‘I’m fine’ but looked like it was covered in blood,” she says. “That’s something somebody could make with a plain T-shirt at home and a Sharpie or a little acrylic paint.”
If you’re still stumped, Ahern suggests calling up your friends and ask what costumes, accessories or props they have. “Swap a couple of pieces and now everybody has something new and is happy and excited – it’s very simple, sustainable, fast.”
Polyglot deliberately uses everyday materials in their performances and experiences as a way to inspire families to continue the creativity in their daily lives.
Simple and open-ended materials, such as paper, scrap fabrics, scarves or tea towels, are “the way to go” for costumes too, Sewell says. It’s a way to come up with ideas and create quickly, without preciousness.
Paper can be folded, twisted and scrunched to create ears, a tail, or “amazing things”, she says. Different paper thicknesses can give varied effects, tissue can be used for colour and volume, and thicker cardboards can create structure and sculptural form.
Packaging or recycling materials can work too, she says. You can paint cereal boxes, or glue on aluminium foil or old wrapping paper to make a robot head, or some sort of a wild hat. You can cut out fangs and stick them on your chin, or make claws for the ends of your fingers. Masking tape, rubber bands and safety pins are excellent tools for attaching and holding.
“There’s so much you can do with what’s lying around in your house. That has more heart and more humanness to it,” she says.
Layers, props, accessories and makeup help build up a character and convey the story. For kids, consider adding a big hat or an oversized jacket from a parent’s wardrobe.
Ahern says a pirate costume can start with a white shirt, some fitted pants and boots. But by layering more elements – a bandana, some eye makeup, lots of necklaces and fingerless gloves – you become more like the character and less like yourself.
A lot of creative things can be done with umbrellas, she says. “I saw somebody once who attached dangly things to the edge of an umbrella and they were a jellyfish.”
Nick Wakerley, a costume designer at Cospro , says a black hooded cloak can belong to any number of characters, but by adding a pair of round black glasses or a scythe you get two very different outcomes.
“A scarf can become a headband or a sash, and a belt can change the shape of something you already own,” he says. “Hair and makeup can do a lot of the work too. Most households have a few makeup and hair products around and getting creative with those can help turn ordinary clothes into a costume.
“You don’t need to cut up or ruin the clothes,” advises Wakerley. “A white shirt, black trousers, slicked back hair and a little red lipstick at the corner of your mouth can give you a vampire. How you move and act can do a lot of the work too.”
The costume designer Paula Levis says you can create something “grotesque and amazing” by combining the dress-up box with household items from the medicine cabinet or hardware and craft supplies.
A child in their regular clothes can be wrapped up in old medical bandages from the back of the cupboard to become a mummy, for instance.
An orange jumper with eyes, nose and mouth fashioned from electrical tape could become a creepy jack o’lantern. Or black clothing with white masking tape could make a face or a skeleton, she says.
Lipstick or food dye can become blood or bruising. A face covered in eyeshadow and a large scrappy or adult-sized shirt can become a zombie.
Almost anything can work, Levis says. “People label themselves as either creative or not from a very young age. I think a lot of parents think: we’re not creative so let’s go to Big W or Kmart. But I think they’ve just got to believe that they can be creative with what they’ve got.”
Adults can want things to be perfect, Sewell says. “Just reusing what you’ve got is the best option for your child’s brain, their wellbeing and development, your connection with them and the planet.”
